title: Incident comms snippets by type (draft) — Customer Success
body:
Doc purpose
- Draft comms snippets keyed by the v1 reliability incident taxonomy. This is meant to help CS/Support communicate clearly and consistently without over-claiming root cause.
- Includes: what we can say / what to avoid, quick questions to ask, and when/how to escalate internally.

Scope / audience
- Audience: Customer Success + Support (especially Dedicated/Private), plus Account teams during escalations.
- Channels: status page, email updates, Slack shared channels, ticket updates.
- This is a draft and will be iterated as taxonomy v1 stabilizes.

Important rules (read before using)
1) Use the incident taxonomy label, not an internal blame statement.
   - Prefer: “Incident type: Capacity/Fleet shortage” over “Routing broke.”
   - If unsure, say “Under investigation; preliminary classification: <type>” and update later.

2) Don’t commit to root cause or a specific fix until Engineering confirms.
   - Avoid statements like “bug in model X” unless explicitly approved by incident commander (IC) / SRE.

3) Time commitments: align with remediation SLA policy.
   - If a customer requests an SLA commitment, reference: “We’re operating under our Dedicated/Private remediation targets; we’ll share next update by <time>.”
   - Don’t promise “fixed in X minutes.” Promise “next update by X” unless you have approval.

4) Share what’s safe: impact + mitigation + customer action.
   - Safe: which product surface is impacted, symptoms, mitigations in progress (failover, rollback, capacity add), workarounds.
   - Be careful: internal architecture details, specific customer identifiers, anything that expands security attack surface.

5) For Dedicated/Private: confirm blast radius.
   - Dedicated: whether single cluster/pool vs multi-tenant components (e.g., control plane) are involved.
   - Private: whether it’s customer-network-specific vs Redwood-managed components. Don’t blame customer configs; ask questions and stay neutral.

6) If security suspicion exists, dual-track.
   - If auth anomalies look suspicious (credential stuffing, unusual IPs, repeated token failures), loop Security Ops per “Security incident alignment” guidance.


How to use taxonomy labels in comms
- Recommended format in internal CS notes (not necessarily customer-facing):
  - Incident type: <top-level type>
  - Subtype (if known): <subtype>
  - Tier affected: Hosted | Dedicated | Private
  - Severity: Sev0/1/2 (internal)

- Recommended format in customer updates (customer-facing):
  - “We’re investigating an issue impacting <symptom> in <region/service>. We’ve identified the issue category as <customer-friendly type phrase> and are implementing mitigations.”

Customer-friendly phrases (use instead of internal labels)
- Availability / 5xx / overload → “elevated error rates” / “service availability degradation”
- Latency regression → “elevated response times”
- Streaming disconnects → “interrupted streaming responses / disconnects”
- Routing / fallback misbehavior → “degraded request routing / failover behavior”
- Capacity / fleet shortage → “capacity constraints affecting throughput”
- Control plane outage → “management/control operations unavailable (policy updates, config changes)”
- Auth / RBAC failures → “authentication/authorization errors”
- Telemetry / blind spot → “monitoring degradation (service may be healthy; visibility reduced)”
- Private connectivity/config issues → “connectivity issues between your environment and Redwood services”


Escalation mapping (CS/Support)
Use this to decide how hard/fast to push internally.

A) Always escalate to SRE / Incident Commander (page if needed)
- Any Dedicated or Private customer reports: sustained 5xx spike, widespread 429s beyond expected quotas, full outage, or repeated streaming disconnects with evidence.
- Any claim of data exposure, suspicious auth patterns, or compromised credentials → Security Ops + SRE.
- Any Sev0/Sev1 incident with unclear blast radius.

B) Escalate to owning team (via incident channel or on-call) after SRE triage
- Routing/fallback misbehavior → Platform Routing on-call.
- Capacity/fleet shortage → Infra/Fleet on-call.
- Runtime regression → Serving Runtime on-call.
- Control plane outage → Platform Control Plane on-call.
- Private connectivity/config issues → Private Deployments + Networking SME.

C) When to involve Account team / leadership
- Dedicated/Private enterprise accounts (contractual commitments, high ARR, regulated workloads): loop Account team after first confirmed customer impact.
- If customer requests formal RCA timeline, service credits, or threatens escalation: loop CS leadership + Product stakeholder for that tier.

D) Minimum customer update cadence (guideline; confirm with IC)
- Sev0/Sev1: first update within 15–30 minutes of confirmation; then every 30–60 minutes or with material change.
- Sev2: first update within ~60 minutes; then every 2–4 hours as appropriate.
- Always set a “next update by <time>” line.


Snippets by incident type
Each section includes: what we can say, what to avoid, questions to ask, and ready-to-send snippets.


1) Availability degradation (5xx spike / overload)
What we can say
- We’re seeing elevated error rates for requests to <endpoint/model> in <region>.
- We are mitigating via traffic shaping, rate limiting adjustments, capacity add, or safe failover.
- We will provide next update by <time>.

What to avoid
- “Your traffic caused the outage.” (Even if overload is driven by a burst; keep neutral.)
- “We hit GPU OOM” / deep internals unless approved.

Questions to ask (quick)
- Affected region(s), time range, sample request IDs.
- Is it all requests or specific model/routes? Any changes on customer side?
- For Dedicated: was there a planned burst / autoscale expectation?

Status page snippet (short)
- “Investigating: Elevated error rates for <product> in <region>. Mitigations in progress. Next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update (medium)
- “We are currently investigating elevated error rates impacting <Hosted/Dedicated/Private> inference requests in <region/cluster>. Our teams have identified this as an availability degradation event and are implementing mitigations (traffic management and capacity stabilization). We will share our next update by <time> or sooner if conditions change.”

Customer action (if relevant)
- If customer can reduce concurrency or retry with backoff: “If possible, reduce peak concurrency and ensure exponential backoff on retries while we stabilize.”


2) Latency regression (p95/p99 elevated)
What we can say
- Response times are elevated; service remains partially/fully available.
- We are working to identify whether the regression is due to load, model rollout, runtime changes, or downstream dependencies.
- Mitigations may include rollback, canary halt, reducing max tokens, adjusting batching.

What to avoid
- “Bad model version” unless confirmed.
- “It’s your prompts” (even if prompt shape contributes; use neutral language).

Questions to ask
- Typical latency baseline vs current; prompt length / max tokens; streaming vs non-streaming.
- Did customer change max_output_tokens, temperature, tools/function calling, or SDK version?

Status page snippet
- “Identified: Elevated response times for <product> in <region>. Working on mitigations; next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We’re observing elevated response times affecting <workload/model> in <region>. The service is responding, but at slower latencies than expected. We are actively investigating and may apply mitigations such as rolling back a change or adjusting capacity/runtime settings. Next update by <time>.”

Optional customer action (only if approved)
- “Temporarily lowering max_output_tokens or reducing concurrent requests may reduce tail latency while we mitigate.”


3) Streaming disconnects / streaming instability
What we can say
- Some streaming responses are disconnecting prematurely; non-streaming may be less impacted.
- We’re checking gateway behavior, network edge, and SDK/client compatibility.
- We can provide recommended client retry behavior (idempotency note).

What to avoid
- “This is the customer’s network” unless confirmed with evidence.
- Overly specific TCP/TLS claims.

Questions to ask
- SDK version, language runtime, proxy/CDN in front, keep-alive settings.
- Do disconnects occur at a consistent time threshold or token count?
- Are they correlated with a recent SDK upgrade? (ref: SUP-18703)

Status page snippet
- “Investigating: Increased rate of streaming disconnects for <product>. Next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We’re investigating an issue where streaming responses may disconnect intermittently. We’re assessing whether the behavior is occurring at the gateway/edge, in a specific region, or related to client/SDK patterns. In the meantime, please ensure retries use exponential backoff and that your application can safely resume or re-issue interrupted requests. Next update by <time>.”

Customer action
- “If you have the option, temporarily switch critical paths to non-streaming requests while we mitigate.”


4) Routing / fallback misbehavior (unexpected model/region/fallback path)
What we can say
- We’re seeing degraded routing/failover behavior leading to increased errors/latency.
- We’re validating routing policy, health signals, and fallback rules.
- Mitigation can include reverting routing policy changes, pinning to a stable route/model, or disabling a problematic fallback.

What to avoid
- “Our router is broken” (too broad); avoid naming internal policy engine specifics.
- “Requests were routed to a cheaper model” (sensitive; can spook customers). Use neutral: “alternate route/model variant.”

Questions to ask
- Are they using pinned model version? Any recent routing policy updates? (ref: SUP-20106 for control plane write failures vs routing)
- Symptoms: wrong region? wrong model? elevated errors during failover?

Status page snippet
- “Identified: Degraded routing/failover behavior impacting <product> in <region>. Mitigations in progress. Next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We have identified an issue affecting request routing/failover behavior for <product>. This may result in elevated error rates or latency for some requests. We are applying mitigations by adjusting routing policies and validating health/fallback signals. Next update by <time>.”

Customer action
- “If your integration supports it, temporarily pin to <region/model> (we can provide recommended settings) until routing is fully stabilized.”


5) Capacity / Fleet shortage (throughput constraints, provisioning lag)
What we can say
- We are experiencing capacity constraints in <region/pool>, impacting throughput and leading to increased 429s/overload behavior.
- We are adding capacity and/or shifting traffic to stabilize.
- For Dedicated: we will confirm whether this is within reserved capacity parameters vs burst behavior.

What to avoid
- “We ran out of GPUs” without context (reads like negligence).
- “Cloud provider can’t deliver” unless explicitly approved; say “upstream provider constraints may be contributing” if needed.

Questions to ask
- For Dedicated: reserved capacity level, expected burst, recent traffic change.
- For Hosted: which region(s) are failing; do they have multi-region configured?
- Are 429s quota-related vs capacity-related? (ref: SUP-19112)

Status page snippet
- “Investigating: Capacity constraints in <region> affecting request throughput. Mitigations in progress; next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We’re currently mitigating capacity constraints impacting throughput in <region/pool>. This may present as elevated 429s or increased error rates during peak load. We are actively adding/stabilizing capacity and validating routing controls to reduce impact. Next update by <time>.”

Customer action (careful)
- “If possible, reduce short-term concurrency or smooth burst traffic while capacity stabilizes. Ensure retries include backoff to avoid amplifying load.”


6) Control plane outage / degraded management operations (policy updates, config writes)
What we can say
- Control/management operations (e.g., updating routing policies, model pins, API keys/RBAC) may be failing.
- Inference/data plane may be healthy; we will confirm.
- Mitigation includes rollback of a control plane change, restoring dependencies, or temporary change freeze.

What to avoid
- “Database is down” / naming internal components.
- “No impact to inference” unless confirmed.

Questions to ask
- What operation is failing? Error messages? Whether inference requests are impacted.
- For enterprise: whether they are blocked on a time-sensitive config change.

Status page snippet
- “Identified: Control plane operations degraded (config changes may fail). Investigating; next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We are investigating an issue affecting management operations (e.g., config/policy updates). Some customers may see failures when attempting to apply changes. We are working to restore normal operation and will confirm whether inference traffic is impacted. Next update by <time>.”

Workaround (if available)
- “If you need an urgent change, reply with the desired configuration and we can coordinate an assisted change path once we confirm safe execution.”


7) Auth / RBAC failures (401/403 spikes, token validation issues)
What we can say
- We are investigating increased authentication/authorization failures.
- Potential mitigations include rolling back auth changes, restoring key validation dependencies, or correcting RBAC policy evaluation.
- We can confirm whether this is widespread vs scoped to specific keys/tenants.

What to avoid
- “Your key is invalid” unless verified.
- Any statement implying compromise without Security involvement.

Questions to ask
- Are all keys failing or only one? Any recent key rotation?
- Are failures region-specific?
- Any unusual IP patterns? (If yes, loop Security Ops.)

Status page snippet
- “Investigating: Increased authentication failures for <product>. Next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We’re investigating increased authentication/authorization failures that may prevent requests from being accepted. We’re working to restore normal auth behavior and will provide guidance if customer action is required (e.g., key re-issuance). Next update by <time>.”

Security handoff trigger
- If there’s any indication of malicious activity: “We are engaging our Security Operations team to assess the pattern in parallel with reliability mitigation.”


8) Telemetry / monitoring blind spot (metrics/logging gaps)
What we can say
- We are experiencing degraded monitoring/telemetry for <region/service>.
- Customer impact may be limited to reporting/visibility; we are validating service health independently.
- We’re restoring telemetry pipelines and ensuring coverage.

What to avoid
- “Everything is fine” (we literally have reduced visibility).
- Detailed monitoring architecture.

Questions to ask
- Is the customer reporting missing metrics/usage data, or are they seeing request failures?
- Which console pages/exports are wrong?

Status page snippet
- “Investigating: Reduced telemetry/metrics visibility for <product>. Service health under validation; next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We are investigating an issue affecting telemetry/visibility (metrics, usage reporting, or dashboards) for <product>. We are validating the underlying service health separately and working to restore normal reporting. Next update by <time>.”


9) Private deployment connectivity/config issues (DNS/TLS/network paths, upgrade-related)
What we can say
- We’re investigating connectivity issues between the customer environment and Redwood services/endpoints.
- We will validate DNS, TLS, routing, allowlists, and any recent upgrades on either side.
- We can provide a targeted checklist and request logs from the customer side.

What to avoid
- “Customer misconfigured DNS” as a first response.
- Over-sharing internal endpoint details; share only what’s required for debugging.

Questions to ask
- When did it start? Any recent upgrade/change (customer or Redwood)? (ref: SUP-19745)
- Specific error: DNS resolution failure, TLS handshake error, timeouts.
- Network path details: egress IPs, firewall rules, proxy.

Status page snippet (only if systemic; many Private customers)
- “Investigating: Connectivity issues affecting some Private deployments. Next update by <time>.”

Email/ticket update
- “We are investigating connectivity errors impacting your Private deployment. We are reviewing DNS/TLS/network path health and any recent changes that may correlate with the onset. To accelerate, please share: timestamp range, affected endpoints, error messages, and sample request IDs (if available). Next update by <time>.”


Comms building blocks (copy/paste)

“Next update” line (universal)
- “Next update by <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM TZ> (or sooner if we have a material change).”

“Impact” line options
- “Impact: elevated error rates for requests to <endpoint/model> in <region>.”
- “Impact: elevated response times for a subset of requests.”
- “Impact: some streaming responses disconnect prematurely.”
- “Impact: management operations (config updates) may fail.”

“Mitigation in progress” line options
- “Mitigation: rolling back a recent change and stabilizing capacity.”
- “Mitigation: adjusting routing/failover policy and validating health signals.”
- “Mitigation: adding capacity and smoothing load via traffic controls.”

“Customer action” safe phrasing
- “If possible, reduce short-term concurrency and ensure retries use exponential backoff.”
- “If available, temporarily route to an alternate region/model configuration; we can provide recommended settings.”


Open questions / TODO (for review)
- TODO: confirm which incident-type phrases are approved for customer-facing comms vs internal-only (especially routing/fallback and model variant wording).
- TODO: align update cadence guidance with SRE incident process doc (Sev0/Sev1 expectations).
- TODO: add dedicated-specific note for distinguishing quota enforcement vs capacity saturation (SUP-19112 learnings).
- TODO: add one example of “good” vs “bad” comms per type (separate appendix?)

Changelog
- 2025-12-10: initial draft created (Rachel) from workshop notes + support escalations.
- 2026-01-22: added control plane + private connectivity sections; linked SUP examples.
- 2026-02-12: tightened ‘what to avoid’ language; added security dual-track trigger reminders.
